titulo: The last morning, and the jacket you left in the taxi
subtitulo: Checking out, leaving the cases behind the hotel desk for the day, and the one sentence that sends a barman to go and look
cena: Twenty to eight in the morning, the case is already in the taxi boot, and your phone is on the counter of the bar where you had the last coffee.

clique.desconto: Nobody handed you those four sentences. You built all four out of one, in an hour, on the way to the airport.
clique.piso: You will get the thing back, because you said the sentence that starts a search. Most people who leave something behind here never ask at all.

frasePiso: You will get the thing back, because you said the sentence that starts a search. Most people who leave something behind here never ask at all.
permissao: You are allowed to say the one Spanish sentence and then carry on in English — the Spanish part is only there to start them looking. You are allowed to leave the cases at the hotel desk after you have handed the key back, and to come for them at six. A last day with nine hours in the middle of it is the ordinary shape of a last day, and that desk sees it every week.
espelho: Apologising for the twenty seconds it takes them to look under the counter is the bit that reads as odd there. Nobody has been put out. You left a thing, they go and look.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You use the word for stolen in the bar where you had breakfast, and the barman's face closes and he starts answering for the bar.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He has gone defensive, so somebody in here probably did take it, and I am not seeing it again.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Two sentences that feel close in English go to different counters here. Me han robado is an accusation and belongs at a police desk; me he dejado says the thing is where you put it, and it is the one that sends somebody to look under the till.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say me he dejado, name the thing, name the place, and then ask whether they have found it.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The bar searches for you instead of defending itself from you, and the search starts in the twenty seconds you are standing there.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a police counter after a real theft. There me han robado is exactly the right sentence and the one the report is written from — that is part seventeen, not this one.

fichasCulturais.sinal: At check-out the desk asks you for another forty-odd euros for nights you already settled online, and sometimes wants it in cash.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have been billed twice, and they have left it to the last morning because they know I am in a hurry.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: A nightly tourist tax exists in Catalonia, the Balearics and, since 2026, the Basque Country. The property collects it for the region, and it is almost never inside the price you paid online.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask whether it is included on the first morning, and keep a few small notes back for the last one.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You leave with the invoice you came for and the taxi still waiting, instead of a conversation at the door with the meter running.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in most of the country. In Madrid or Andalusia nobody asks you for it, because there is nothing there to ask for.

steps.pt: Part eighteen, and it is the last one. Warm-up: metronome hand. One tap a syllable, all the same size.
De-ja-do. Three taps, three the same. English swallows the middle one. The hand will not let you.

steps.promptPt: Something from last night's goodbye dinner is still arguing with you, and there is a green cross two doors down. Ask the woman behind that counter. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de estómago?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh rreh-koh-men-DAR AL-goh PAH-rah el doh-LOR deh ehs-TOH-mah-goh
steps.pt: something for that
Twenty to eight in the morning. The case is already in the taxi boot, and you are patting your pockets.
Your phone is on the counter of the bar where you had the last coffee. You have about eleven minutes.
There are two ways to say that here, and only one of them ends with the phone back in your hand.

steps.es: Me han robado el móvil.
steps.pinyin: meh ahn rroh-BAH-dhoh el MOH-beel
steps.pt: 👂 'My phone has been stolen.' — the police counter sentence, and part seventeen's, not this morning's.
steps.tts: Me han robado el móvil.

steps.es: Me he dejado el móvil en el bar.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh el MOH-beel en el bar
steps.pt: I've left my phone in the bar. — nobody did anything to you; it is where you put it.
steps.tts: Me he dejado el móvil en el bar.

steps.pt: The frame is me he dejado — the one from the taxi on night one. It never moves. Then the thing, then where.

steps.es: Me he dejado la chaqueta en el taxi.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh lah chah-KEH-tah en el TAK-see
steps.pt: I've left my jacket in the taxi.
steps.tts: Me he dejado la chaqueta en el taxi.

steps.pt: Two little pieces: the thing, and then where. En el taxi. En el tren. En la habitación. Aquí.

steps.promptPt: Back on the pavement outside that bar, eleven minutes left, and the barman is already looking at you. Say what is on his counter, and where. Speak now.
steps.es: Me he dejado el móvil en el bar.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh el MOH-beel en el bar
steps.pt: left it behind, and where
Said that way, a barman goes and looks. Said the other way, he stops looking and starts defending his bar.

steps.promptPt: You are in the lift going down, and whatever it was that opened the door upstairs is still lying on the bed. Tell the desk as you land. Speak now.
steps.es: Me he dejado las llaves en la habitación.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh lahs YAH-behs en lah ah-bee-tah-THYON
steps.pt: upstairs, on the bed
steps.tts: Me he dejado las llaves en la habitación.

steps.pt: And there is a second half to it, four words long, which is what turns your sentence into their search.

steps.es: ¿Lo han encontrado?
steps.pinyin: loh ahn en-kon-TRAH-dhoh
steps.pt: Has anyone found it? — ask it straight after, in the same breath.
steps.tts: ¿Lo han encontrado?

steps.promptPt: The little office at the rank, and last night's receipt is in your hand with the car number on it. Tell them what is on the back seat, and where. Speak now.
steps.es: Me he dejado la chaqueta en el taxi.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh lah chah-KEH-tah en el TAK-see
steps.pt: on the back seat, and where

steps.es: ¿Tiene el recibo?
steps.pinyin: TYEH-neh el rreh-THEE-boh
steps.pt: 👂 'Have you got the receipt?' — the slip you asked for on the way in. It is the car number.
steps.tts: ¿Tiene el recibo?

steps.promptPt: He asks for the bit of paper you took when you got out that night, and it is in your wallet. Four words and a nod. Speak now.
steps.es: Sí, aquí lo tengo.
steps.pinyin: see, ah-KEE loh TEN-goh
steps.pt: yes — here it is
steps.tts: Sí, aquí lo tengo.

steps.pt: And for the thing you have never known the word for, there is una cosa — a thing — plus your screen.
Lo for the phone, la for the jacket. That little word moves with the thing, and no jacket was ever lost over it.

steps.promptPt: Whatever it is called in Spanish, you have never known. You are back at the counter with a photo of it on your screen. Say you left one here, ask, and show them. Speak now.
steps.es: Me he dejado una cosa aquí. ¿La han encontrado?
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh OO-nah KOH-sah ah-KEE · lah ahn en-kon-TRAH-dhoh
steps.pt: no word needed, and the photo does the rest
steps.tts: Me he dejado una cosa aquí. ¿La han encontrado?

steps.pt: Now rewind an hour, to the hotel desk. Checking out is three sentences and about four minutes.

steps.promptPt: He turns the screen round with the whole week on it, waiting for a card. You settled every night of it online back in March. Three words. Speak now.
steps.es: Ya está pagado.
steps.pinyin: yah ehs-TAH pah-GAH-dhoh
steps.pt: that one is already done
steps.tts: Ya está pagado.

steps.es: Sí, aquí me sale pagado. Solo queda la tasa turística.
steps.pinyin: see, ah-KEE meh SAH-leh pah-GAH-dhoh. SOH-loh KEH-dhah lah TAH-sah too-REES-tee-kah
steps.pt: 👂 'Yes, it shows as paid. Only the tourist tax left.' — that one is charged at the desk, not by the website.
steps.tts: Sí, aquí me sale pagado. Solo queda la tasa turística.

steps.pt: Ya está — it is already — and then the one word saying which. Pagado. Reservado. Hecho. Incluido.

steps.promptPt: Somebody at work will want to see this week on paper, with the hotel's name across the top. Ask before he closes the screen. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me puede dar la factura, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh dar lah fak-TOO-rah, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: the paper one, with the name on it
steps.tts: ¿Me puede dar la factura, por favor?

steps.es: ¿A nombre de quién?
steps.pinyin: ah NOM-breh deh kyen
steps.pt: 👂 'In whose name?' — a factura carries your name; a tique does not, and the insurer wants the one with the name.
steps.tts: ¿A nombre de quién?

steps.promptPt: Out of the room at eleven, flight at nine tonight, and two heavy things you do not fancy dragging round a city. You will come back for them at six. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Puedo dejar las maletas hasta las seis?
steps.pinyin: PWEH-dhoh deh-KHAR lahs mah-LEH-tahs AHS-tah lahs says
steps.pt: until six, behind the desk
steps.tts: ¿Puedo dejar las maletas hasta las seis?

steps.pt: One line on that bill you did not put there: a tax per night, and it is not inside what you paid online.
Catalonia, the Balearics, and the Basque Country since twenty twenty-six. In Madrid or Seville, nothing.

steps.es: ¿La tasa turística está incluida?
steps.pinyin: lah TAH-sah too-REES-tee-kah ehs-TAH een-kloo-EE-dhah
steps.pt: Is the tourist tax included? — you asked this on day one, which is why it is a line and not a shock.
It is often cash, at the desk, on the way out. Keep two small notes back for it and it takes ten seconds.
Outside, the car. Same question as the night you landed, in the same order, before the boot closes.

steps.promptPt: The rank outside the hotel, the airport an hour away, and he has not touched the meter. Settle what it comes to before you get in. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Es tarifa fija al aeropuerto?
steps.pinyin: es tah-REE-fah FEE-khah al ah-eh-roh-PWEHR-toh
steps.pt: is it the flat one, out there
steps.tts: ¿Es tarifa fija al aeropuerto?

steps.es: Fija, sí. Si vamos dentro de la M-30.
steps.pinyin: FEE-khah, see. see BAH-mohs DEN-troh deh lah EH-meh TRAYN-tah
steps.pt: 👂 'Fixed, yes — if we're going inside the M-30.' — the flat airport fare stops at the ring road.
steps.tts: Fija, sí. Si vamos dentro de la eme treinta.

steps.pt: In Madrid it is thirty-three euros between Barajas and anywhere inside the M-thirty, any hour, nothing added.
Going out by train instead? One window, one sentence, and the opener you have had since the bakery.

steps.promptPt: Cercanías, half seven, and the machine has a queue you have not got time for. The window is open, the man is waiting, and there are two of you going where the planes are. Speak now.
steps.es: Quería dos billetes para el aeropuerto.
steps.pinyin: keh-REE-ah dohs bee-YEH-tehs PAH-rah el ah-eh-roh-PWEHR-toh
steps.pt: two, and where to
steps.tts: Quería dos billetes para el aeropuerto.

steps.pt: If there is a hire car, give yourself an extra half hour and fill the tank before you reach the counter.

steps.promptPt: He walks round the car with a tablet, says everything is in order, and turns to go. You would like that sentence somewhere other than his mouth. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me lo puede dar por escrito, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh dar por ehs-KREE-toh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: on paper, please
At the airport, the machine that took four fingerprints off you on the way in logs you going out, too.
It has you on file now, so this pass is the quick one. Same queue, a fraction of the time.
GUIRI ALERT, and it is the last one, so let us make it count. The owner comes out and asks if you liked the food.
You mean absolutely, so you say en absoluto. You have just told him: not in the slightest. Not one bit.
It is the one that flips on you. What you wanted was totalmente. Or desde luego. Say them once, out loud.

steps.es: ¡Totalmente! Desde luego.
steps.pinyin: toh-tal-MEN-teh · DEHS-deh LWEH-goh
steps.pt: Absolutely! Of course. — the two that mean what you thought the other one meant.
steps.tts: ¡Totalmente! Desde luego.

steps.pt: One thing left, and it is the one everybody skips. The bar you stood in every morning of this week.

steps.es: Ha estado genial. Volveré.
steps.pinyin: ah ehs-TAH-dhoh kheh-NYAL · bol-beh-REH
steps.pt: It's been great. I'll come back.
steps.tts: Ha estado genial. Volveré.

steps.pt: Not a speech. Two short ones at the counter, on your way past, with the case still in your hand.

steps.promptPt: The man who has made your coffee every day since Monday, and thirty seconds before the taxi goes. Tell him how it was, and that this is not the end of it. Speak now.
steps.es: Ha estado genial. Volveré.
steps.pinyin: ah ehs-TAH-dhoh kheh-NYAL · bol-beh-REH
steps.pt: how it was, and that you'll be back

steps.es: Muchas gracias por todo. Hasta la próxima.
steps.pinyin: MOO-chahs GRAH-thyahs por TOH-dhoh · AHS-tah lah PROK-see-mah
steps.pt: Thank you for everything. Until the next time.
steps.tts: Muchas gracias por todo. Hasta la próxima.

steps.promptPt: The woman at the desk who kept your bags all afternoon and rang for the car. Longer than a nod, and it is the last thing you say in this building. Speak now.
steps.es: Muchas gracias por todo. Hasta la próxima.
steps.pinyin: MOO-chahs GRAH-thyahs por TOH-dhoh · AHS-tah lah PROK-see-mah
steps.pt: for all of it — and until next time
And you may say your sentence and then carry on in English. The Spanish part is what starts them looking.
You may also leave the cases after you hand the key back and come for them at six. That desk sees it weekly.
Count the places, not the phrases. The bar. The lift going down. The taxi office. The counter with the photo.
Nobody handed you those four sentences. You built all four out of one, in an hour, on the way to the airport.
You will get the thing back, because you said the sentence that starts a search. Most people never ask at all.
Shadowing. Over the top of them, out loud, hand going. One for the morning, one for the door.

steps.es: Me he dejado el móvil en el bar.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh el MOH-beel en el bar
steps.pt: I've left my phone in the bar.

steps.pinyin: ah ehs-TAH-dhoh kheh-NYAL · bol-beh-REH
steps.pt: It's been great. I'll come back.
One more, out loud, on a platform where we have not put anything down yet. Then we are done.

steps.promptPt: Atocha, the doors have shut behind you, and you are one short of what you got on with in Seville. The man in the red waistcoat is right there. Speak now.
steps.es: Me he dejado la maleta en el tren.
steps.pinyin: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh lah mah-LEH-tah en el tren
steps.pt: the big one, and where
steps.tts: Me he dejado la maleta en el tren.

steps.pt: That is Get by, all eighteen. You arrive, you order, you pay, you sleep — and you go home with your jacket.

aprofundar.titulo: The last morning, in order (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: 'Me he dejado' and 'me han robado' go to different counters
secoes.corpo: Spanish keeps two clean sentences where English blurs one. 'Me he dejado el móvil en el bar' says the thing is where you put it and nobody did anything wrong; it is an appeal for help and the person hearing it has no reason to feel accused, which is exactly why they go and look. 'Me han robado el móvil' says somebody took it; it is the sentence a police report is written from, it is the one your insurer needs, and it is taught in part seventeen for that reason. Say the second one in a bar and you will usually get a defence rather than a search — not because anyone is touchy, but because you have just described a crime in their premises. The frame takes an object and a place, and the object list is short enough to hold in your head: el móvil, la chaqueta, las llaves, la maleta, el pasaporte. The places are en el taxi, en el tren, en la habitación, en el bar, and the shortest of all, aquí. Add '¿lo han encontrado?' straight afterwards — 'has anyone found it?' — and the sentence stops being an announcement and becomes a request. If the thing is feminine, the little word changes to 'la han encontrado', and nobody has ever failed to find a jacket because a visitor said 'lo' instead of 'la'.

exemplos.es: Me he dejado el pasaporte en la habitación.
exemplos.pt: meh eh deh-KHAH-dhoh el pah-sah-POR-teh — I've left my passport in the room.

exemplos.es: Me he dejado una cosa aquí. ¿La han encontrado?
exemplos.pt: OO-nah KOH-sah ah-KEE — I've left a thing here. Has anyone found it? (with the photo on your screen, this is a complete sentence)

secoes.titulo: Check-out, and the tax that is not on your booking
secoes.corpo: Three sentences do the desk: 'Ya está pagado' if you settled online, '¿Me puede dar la factura, por favor?' for the itemised bill with the property's name on it, and '¿Puedo dejar las maletas hasta las seis?' for the gap between the room and the flight. Note that leaving the cases is a normal request and not a favour — the luggage room exists because everybody's flight is at nine. The one thing that surprises people is the nightly tourist tax. It exists in Catalonia, the Balearics and, since 2026, the Basque Country; the property collects it on behalf of the region, it is generally not inside what you paid on a booking site, and it is often asked for in cash at the desk on the way out. In most of Spain there is no such tax at all, which is why it feels like an invention when it appears. The defence is not an argument, it is a question asked on the first morning — '¿La tasa turística está incluida?' — so that on the last morning it is a line you were expecting. Barcelona sits at the top end of the scale, where the total for a five-star hotel reached twelve euros a night in April 2026 and the municipal part of it is on a published schedule to keep rising to 2029.

exemplos.pt: seh PAH-gah ah-PAR-teh — Is the tax paid separately?

exemplos.es: ¿Puedo dejar las maletas hasta las seis?
exemplos.pt: deh-KHAR lahs mah-LEH-tahs — Can I leave the cases until six?

secoes.titulo: The ride out, the hire car, and the machine at the border
secoes.corpo: Going out is the same conversation as coming in, with the questions in the same order: '¿Está libre?', the address on the screen rather than in your accent, and the fare settled before the boot shuts. In Madrid there is nothing to negotiate — a taxi between Barajas and any address inside the M-30 is a fixed thirty-three euros, twenty-four hours a day, with no surcharges permitted, which is why '¿Es tarifa fija al aeropuerto?' is a confirmation rather than a haggle. If you are returning a hire car, the two things that cost money are the tank and the paperwork: fill it before you arrive if the contract is full-to-full, and when the man with the tablet says everything is in order, ask for that in writing — '¿Me lo puede dar por escrito, por favor?' The pressure at that counter is verbal by design, and a sentence in writing is the only kind that survives the drive home. Ask also when the deposit comes back off the card. At the border, the same system that photographed you and took four fingerprints on the way in records your exit; the profile already exists, so the second pass is much faster than the first. It also means the ninety-days-in-any-one-hundred-and-eighty count is now automatic, and your exit date is part of it.

exemplos.pt: KWAN-doh meh loh deh-BWEL-behn — When do I get it back? (the deposit blocked on your card)
es YEH-noh ah YEH-noh — Is it full-to-full? (the only fuel policy worth having)

secoes.titulo: Saying goodbye to people who served you all week
secoes.corpo: The last thing is the cheapest thing in the course and the one most visitors skip: a sentence to the bar that fed you every morning. 'Ha estado genial' — it's been great — and 'Volveré' — I'll come back. Add 'Muchas gracias por todo' at the hotel desk and 'Hasta la próxima' on the way out of the door, and you have done in fifteen seconds what a card and a tip do not do. 'Hasta luego' is the ordinary goodbye and it does not commit you to returning later that day — it is what you say on the way out of a shop, even to someone you will never see again, and 'Adiós' does the same job. Keep 'en absoluto' out of your mouth entirely on this last morning: it looks like 'absolutely' and it means 'not in the slightest', so the enthusiastic answer to '¿Le ha gustado?' turns into a flat no in front of the person who cooked it. What you want is '¡Totalmente!' or 'Desde luego'. And if you are asked whether you will be back, the honest answer, said out loud, tends to be the one that gets remembered next year.

exemplos.pt: AHS-tah lah PROK-see-mah — Until the next time.
keh ohs BAH-yah mwee byen — All the best to you (said to the pair of them behind the counter)
